messages.content: 请检索以下问题的相关原文：关于论文《A Readable Read: Automatic Assessment of Language Learning Materials based on Linguistic Complexity》，what linguistics features did they apply?

claims.text: The authors developed their features based on previous literature and a grammar book for Swedish L2 learners.
The feature set is divided into five subgroups: length-based, lexical, morphological, syntactic and semantic features.
Length-based features include sentence length in tokens and characters, extra-long words (longer than thirteen characters) and the traditional Swedish readability formula LIX.

Lexical features used information from the Kelly list, a lexical resource providing a CEFR level and frequencies per lemma; the authors used incidence scores per 1000 words, incidence scores of words at each CEFR level, difficult tokens above the text's CEFR level, tokens not in the Kelly list, tokens without a lemma, and average log frequencies.

Morphological features included variation and incidence scores of lexical categories, punctuations, particles, sub- and conjunctions, fine-grained inflectional information (e.g., neuter gender nouns and verb form ratios), bilogarithmic and square root type-token ratios, nominal ratio, pronoun-to-preposition ratio, lexical density measures, and relative structures.
Syntactic features were based on the length (depth) and direction of dependency arcs, incidence scores of relative clauses in clefts, and incidence scores of pre- and postmodifiers.
Semantic features were based on SALDO, a Swedish lexical-semantic resource, using the average number of senses per token and the average number of noun senses per noun.
At the document level, using lexical features alone achieved approximately the same performance (0.8 F) as the complete feature set (0.81 F).
Combining different features rather than using lexical features alone resulted in a 7% improvement in classification accuracy at the sentence level.
